citeAs: Pierre-Carl Langlais, Carlos Rosas Hinostroza, Mattia Nee, Catherine Amett, Pavel Chizhov, Eliot Krzystof Jones, Irène Girard, David Mach, Anastasia Stasenko, Ivan P. Yamshchikov (2025). Common Corpus: The Largest Collection of Ethical Data for LLM Pre-Training. arXiv:2506.01732.
creator: Pierre-Carl Langlais, Carlos Rosas Hinostroza, Mattia Nee, Catherine Amett, Pavel Chizhov, Eliot Krzystof Jones, Irène Girard, David Mach, Anastasia Stasenko, Ivan P. Yamshchikov (PleIAs)
description: Common Corpus is the largest open dataset for language model pre-training, containing approximately 2 trillion tokens (~1,998,647,168,282 tokens). The data is either uncopyrighted or under permissible licenses, and covers a wide variety of languages (from major European languages to low-resource ones) as well as code data, spanning diverse genres, time periods, and domains across six collections: Open Government, Open Culture, Open Science, Open Code, Open Web, and Open Semantic.
inLanguage: en, fr, de, es, la, it, pl, el, pt, ru, nl, da, sv, cs, sr, ar, bn, fa, sa, ur, lb, and many others (300+ languages including low-resource languages)
license: Multiple licenses per document; the ten most common are: Public Domain, CC-BY, MIT, CC-BY-SA, Apache-2.0, BSD-3-Clause, Open license, BSD-2-Clause, CC-BY-4.0, CC0-1.0. License metadata is provided per document in the dataset.
name: Common Corpus
rai:dataBiases: The paper acknowledges several biases: (1) Language bias — despite multilingual coverage, low-resource languages still have shallow coverage; African languages (e.g., Swahili, Wolof, Bambara) are underrepresented. (2) English dominance — Open Science collection has ~85% English documents due to the specificity of open scientific publishing. (3) Historical bias — Open Culture contains many historical texts (18th-19th centuries) with cultural norms that do not meet modern ethical standards, including harmful language about ethnic groups, women, and violence; this is partially mitigated by toxicity filtering. (4) Web data bias — Common Crawl was shown to contain sexual content, hate speech, and racial and gender biases. (5) The dataset does not contain instruction-tuning data, limiting its direct use for task-specific fine-tuning.
rai:dataCollection: Common Corpus was assembled from six major collections: (1) Open Government — financial, legal, and administrative data in the public domain from sources such as SEC, WTO, AMF, TED EU Tenders, GATT Library, Europarl, Caselaw Access Project, CourtListener, EUR-lex, Eurovoc, French Open Data, USPTO, UN Digital Library, and OECD; (2) Open Culture — cultural heritage datasets (monographs and periodicals) from Collections As Data (CAD) initiatives, Internet Archive, Delpher, Gallica, Chronicling America, Europeana, and various national libraries; (3) Open Science — scientific papers and documents collected via OpenAlex API filtered by CC-By, Public Domain/CC0, and CC-By-SA licenses, plus arXiv and European-specific resources; (4) Open Code — code data from The Stack v1 and v2; (5) Open Web — Wikipedia, Wikisource (via Wikimedia Enterprise HTML dumps), YouTube Commons (CC-By audio transcripts), and StackExchange; (6) Open Semantic — Wikidata in natural language, covering 300 languages, developed in collaboration with Wikimedia Deutschland.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources include: PDF documents (over 1.36 million original PDFs from AMF and WTO), digitized text from national libraries (Gallica, Library of Congress, Europeana, Delpher, etc.), raw XML output (METS/ALTO format), mediawiki syntax from Wikimedia projects, source code files from GitHub (via The Stack v1 and v2), audio transcripts from YouTube, RDF triples from Wikidata, and structured legal/administrative documents from government databases.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Source documents span from 1618 (Europeana Newspapers) to 2024 (SEC reports, WTO documents). Dataset development began in May 2023; first published as Common Corpus in March 2024; current version released in February 2025 for the Paris AI Summit.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web API, Web Scraping, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: Known limitations include: (1) The dataset does not cover the full range of available open data (the "open data paradox" — most content under free licenses is not integrated into existing pretraining datasets). (2) Low-resource language coverage is still shallow. (3) The ~2 trillion tokens is suitable for pre-training models of limited size; larger models require significantly more data. (4) The dataset does not contain instruction-tuning data and is not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning. (5) Curation methods (OCR correction, toxicity detection, PII removal) cannot achieve 100% accuracy. (6) OCR errors remain in some documents. (7) None of the curation methods can guarantee complete removal of all problematic content.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For Open Culture data: toxic/harmful content is either removed or synthetically rewritten without the harmful language using the Celadon classifier pipeline. For Wikidata (Open Semantic): RDF triples were translated into natural language sequences (e.g., "Q41309 | P:27 | Q171150" becoming "Franz Liszt country of citizenship Kingdom of Hungary"), with all available translations provided as consecutive blocks separated by newlines. A "refined" version for late training of about 1 trillion tokens was derived with more intensive, curation-based filtering.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing steps include: (1) Text segmentation using Segmentext, a model trained to handle broken/unstructured texts with digitization artifacts; (2) OCR quality assessment using OCRoscope (based on cld2 language identification, measuring non-recognized 7-grams) and OCRerrcr (a DeBERTa-v2-style model with 400M parameters); (3) OCR correction using OCRonos (based on Llama 3 8B), correcting OCR errors, wrong word cuts/merges, and broken text structures; (4) PII removal using Microsoft's Presidio with custom regular expression patterns, replacing PII with fictitious but realistic values; (5) Toxicity detection using Celadon (a DeBERTa-v3-small model ~140M parameters trained on 2M annotated samples) identifying toxic content along five dimensions; (6) For Open Code: removal of unwanted file types (SVG, csv, json, etc.), license filtering, removal of files with 75%+ digits, and replacement of [\r]+\n sequences; (7) Language identification using the fastText language identification model.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Common Corpus is described as "an evolving resource reflecting the need for a continuous open infrastructure rather than a fixed dataset." HuggingFace ensures proper archiving of past versions for reproducibility. Ongoing collection of more data in European languages is planned as part of the LLMs4EU project. Future enlargement of corpora in African languages (e.g., Swahili, Wolof, Bambara) is planned.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Common Corpus aims to support open and auditable LLM development that is legally compliant with AI legislation including EU AI regulations, enabling open science research without relying on copyrighted or proprietary content. It is described as a critical infrastructure for open science research in LLMs, analogous to a shared research infrastructure as defined by UNESCO. It has been used by industry leaders (Anthropic) and multiple European LLM projects. The dataset contributes to making French and other European languages high-resource for LLM training. It was acknowledged as one of the main deliverables of the Paris AI Summit 2025 as the "largest open database to train Large Language Models." The paper argues it demonstrates that LLM development is possible while meeting legal and regulatory requirements even under strict EU AI regulations.
rai:dataUseCases: Intended use cases include: (1) Pre-training of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Small Language Models (SLMs); (2) Multilingual language model development; (3) Development of models for creative writing; (4) Historical language model development; (5) Legal knowledge models and document processing for administrative applications; (6) Vision-language models (VLMs) for document segmentation and processing; (7) Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) models; (8) Code generation and reasoning models; (9) Speech foundation models (via YouTube Commons); (10) Multimodal dataset creation; (11) Open science research on LLMs. The dataset can be used on its own or in conjunction with existing open datasets.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Several machine/ML tools were used in the pipeline: (1) Segmentext — a custom model for text segmentation trained to handle digitization artifacts; (2) OCRoscope — a tool based on the cld2 language identification tool for OCR quality assessment; (3) OCRerrcr — a DeBERTa-v2-style language model with 400M parameters for OCR error detection; (4) OCRonos — a model based on Llama 3 8B for OCR correction; (5) Microsoft Presidio — an open-source tool for PII identification and replacement; (6) Celadon — a DeBERTa-v3-small model (~140M parameters) trained on 2M annotated samples for multilingual toxicity detection; (7) fastText language identification model for language distribution computation; (8) OpenAlex API for filtering scientific documents by license.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) was identified and removed. PII types addressed include phone numbers, email addresses, and IP addresses. Microsoft's Presidio was used to identify and replace PII with fictitious but realistic values. Custom regular expression patterns were applied to increase detection accuracy for phone numbers from ~55-60% to ~85%.

null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: No annotation quality analysis or inter-annotator agreement metrics are described; the dataset is not manually annotated.
